opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because I've been in a few different kinds of environments: academia, and then spending time closer to industry labs. The main thing is that a good research environment has to tolerate a portfolio of bets. There's a strong pull right now toward everyone working on the same thing, scaling the same kind of model and chasing the same benchmarks. Some of that is rational, because those directions are clearly producing results. But if everyone converges, you lose the people who are going to find the next thing, or who will explain why the current thing works at all.

So practically, I think it means a few things. First, protecting time and resources for work that doesn't look immediately impressive. Many of the ideas that matter, whether in efficient architectures, new ways of thinking about inference, or theory, look kind of small or weird at first. If a student or researcher has to justify every project by whether it beats the state of the art in six months, you'll filter those out.

Second, I think it's about the culture of conversation. People working on very different things should actually talk to each other and take each other seriously. The systems person, the theory person, and the person training big models all have something to learn from each other. Some of my favorite projects came from someone saying, "Wait, why does that work?" from a totally different angle.

And third, especially in academia, I think we should lean into our comparative advantage rather than trying to imitate industry. We're not going to win on compute. But we can be the place where people take longer-horizon risks, build open tools, and do careful science. Supporting that means valuing things like good software, good evaluations, and clear explanations, not just papers with big numbers.

Honestly, a lot of it just comes down to advisors and senior people signaling that it's okay to work on something different, and then actually backing that up when it comes time for hiring, funding, and recognition.

r001.rationale: The response says people working on different things should talk, take each other seriously, and learn from different angles when developing projects.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a good research environment must tolerate “a portfolio of bets.”

r003.rationale: It recommends protecting resources for less immediately impressive work and supporting longer-horizon risks.

r004.rationale: It values good evaluations, but does not call for the research community to agree on empirical criteria for assessing research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, partly because I've sat in a few different kinds of environments — academia at Cornell, and then time at places like Hugging Face and inside industry labs — and they each get this wrong in their own way.

The honest answer is that a lot of the value of a research environment is just that it lets people be stubborn for a while. Most interesting directions look bad for a long time before they look good. If you'd asked me around 2018 whether people should keep working on things like efficient inference or structured decoding or small models, the conventional answer was "no, just scale," and a lot of the time that answer was right. But the environments that produced the most interesting work were the ones that tolerated a few people ignoring that advice.

So concretely, I think a good environment does a couple of things. One is that it lowers the cost of trying something. In NLP right now a huge part of that is compute and infrastructure. If every student has to spend three months building a training pipeline before they can test an idea, you've effectively filtered out every idea that isn't worth three months upfront, which is most of them. I'm a big believer in shared tooling, open-source baselines, that kind of thing — it's not glamorous but it's what makes the "weird" project cheap enough to attempt.

The second thing is that it protects people from the gravitational pull of whatever the hot thing is. In a group with a strong central agenda, everyone drifts toward it, and that's fine for a while, but you end up with a monoculture. I've tried, with my own students, to be pretty explicit that I don't want everyone working on the same problem. It's harder to advise, honestly — you have to actually learn what they're doing instead of just pattern-matching to your own work — but you get a much more interesting group.

And the third thing, which I think gets underrated, is that different directions need different kinds of feedback. Someone doing careful systems work needs a very different reviewer than someone doing a speculative theory project. A good environment has enough range in it that people can find the right critic, and it has a culture where being critical is a form of taking someone's work seriously rather than a way of shutting them down.

What I'd push back on a little is the idea that "supporting many directions" means being hands-off. I think it actually means being more engaged, not less — you're just engaged on the terms of each person's problem instead of on the terms of your own.

r001.rationale: The response supports researchers pursuing different problems, but does not recommend bringing people with different perspectives into the process of shaping research directions.

r002.rationale: It argues against everyone working on the same problem and says a group should support different directions, describing a varied set of ideas within the group’s agenda.

r003.rationale: It endorses letting people stay with directions that look bad for a long time and tolerating researchers who ignore conventional advice.

r004.rationale: It calls for different kinds of feedback and appropriate critics, but does not call for community agreement on empirical criteria for assessing research.

astra-6.text:
I think a good research environment should give people room to develop their own taste. Some people want to build systems, some want to understand a phenomenon, and some want to work on something that might not pay off for a few years. You want those people to be able to talk to each other without feeling that they all have to work on the same thing.

That doesn’t mean you don’t challenge each other. You should ask hard questions: Why is this interesting? What would we learn if it worked? But there’s a difference between helping someone make their idea stronger and steering them toward the project you would have chosen. As an advisor or a colleague, I think you want to do more of the former. Give people support and useful feedback, and leave enough space for them to surprise you.

r001.rationale: It encourages people pursuing different kinds of work to talk, but does not recommend involving different perspectives in shaping research directions.

r002.rationale: It supports individuals developing distinct interests, but does not frame the group's agenda as a portfolio of ideas.

r003.rationale: It explicitly supports people working on ideas that might not pay off for a few years.

r004.rationale: It calls for hard questions and useful feedback, but says nothing about agreeing on empirical criteria for evaluating research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a good research environment gives people room to develop their own taste. Some people want to understand a very specific question deeply; other people want to build something and see what happens. You want both of those people to feel like their work is valued, without forcing everybody into the same way of doing research.

That takes a combination of freedom and engagement. You should be able to pursue a direction that other people aren’t immediately excited about, but you should also have colleagues who will listen carefully, challenge your assumptions, and help you figure out what would make the work compelling. Giving someone independence shouldn’t mean leaving them on their own.

r001.rationale: The response values different research styles and supportive colleagues, but does not recommend involving people with different perspectives in shaping research directions.

r002.rationale: It supports varied individual approaches, but does not frame the group’s agenda as a portfolio of ideas.

r003.rationale: It encourages pursuing a direction others may not immediately favor, but does not address ideas with low probabilities of success.

r004.rationale: The response says colleagues should challenge assumptions, but does not call for shared empirical criteria for assessing research.
